title: Paramitas, Tonglen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett steps away from koan study for a week to introduce the six paramitas, which six senior students will each take up in July talks while Nomon is on sabbatical. Nomon reads the opening of Norman Fischer's book The World Could Be Otherwise, where the poet Robert Desnos reads palms in a line of prisoners headed for the gas chambers, predicting long lives and joy until the guards cannot carry out the executions. Nomon connects this story of imagination to the bodhisattva path, then leads a tonglen meditation: breathing in suffering as dark smoke, first one's own, then a friend's, then a whole group's, and breathing out light.

I was just having a nice meeting with our senior students, practice leaders who have been to shuso.
They've all agreed to give talks and run the zendo in the month of July while I'm taking sabbatical.
We've been starting to study some books on the six paramitas, the six practices of bodhisattvas, so we decided that six of them would give six talks on the six paramitas.
Just to remind you, these are the six guideposts and main practices of bodhisattvas.
It would be good for all of us to have them on the tip of our tongue and remind ourselves a lot.
First is generosity, dana paramita.
Then the precepts, ethical living, sila paramita or shila paramita.
Then patience and forbearance.
We need a lot of that these days, yeah.
That's khyanti paramita.
Then energy.
Norman actually translates it as enthusiastic energy, yes, which is virya paramita.
Then there's meditation, which is jhana paramita, derived from that word.
And then wisdom, prajnaparamita.

Of course there's all this interesting discussion in the tradition about how this isn't just conventional wisdom and compassion and generosity and so on, but really understanding these things deeply, in the light of the real nature of the way things are.
So paramita sometimes is translated as "going beyond": the generosity that goes beyond being generosity, the patience that goes beyond being patience.
One of the books that we're studying, which I recommend everybody read and study, is a recent book by Norman called The World Could Be Otherwise.
He gave a little book talk about this last summer, I think it was.
Was that really this last summer?
Yeah, that seems so long ago.
One of the interesting things that Norman does, which I have not heard other people do quite as much, is emphasize imagination as a fundamental quality of spiritual practice and religious life.
So tonight I thought I would share with you the opening of his book on the paramitas, and this fabulous little story that he holds up as a great example of the way imagination can shift reality.
The imagination isn't just making it up.
It's to do with the fundamental way we look at things and feel about things and relate to each other.
I think it also reminds us that we're making it all up anyway, you know what I mean?
The reality we're constructing, based on our senses and our thinking and our culture, is a shared project of making things up.
It is a very imaginative act to imagine ourselves, to imagine the world.

So I thought I'd share the beginning of this, and then I thought we might do a led meditation, which we don't usually do, and which has always struck me as one of the more imaginative Buddhist meditations.
We'll get to that.
Here's the opening of Norman's book.
It's about three or four pages, and it's a story he's going to tell us.
Everybody hearing okay?
The sound is okay now?
Okay, good.
So this is Norman reading this story.
*Here's a story about how imagination changes the world, even in the worst possible circumstances.
It involves the French surrealist poet Robert Desnos.
Desnos was Jewish and during World War II he went underground to fight for the resistance.
He was captured and sent to the concentration camps.
One day, along with many other men, Desnos is crowded into the back of one of the trucks that transports prisoners from the barracks.
The men fully understand where they're going.
The trucks always leave the barracks full and return empty.
Their destination is the gas chambers and the ovens.
No one in the truck speaks.
The mood is resigned, stricken, eyes are lowered, faces grim.
When the truck arrives, the prisoners slowly and silently descend as if in a dream.
The guards, normally full of jokes and banter, fell silent, unable to avoid catching the prisoners' mood.*
*But this almost religious silence is abruptly interrupted.
One of the men in the line of prisoners suddenly, with great animation, jumps up, pivots, and grabs the hand of a man behind him.
Astonishingly, his nose almost touching the man's hand, his body coiled with energy, he begins to read the man's palm.
I'm so excited for you, he exclaims happily.
You are going to live a long and happy life.
You're going to have three more children and a beautiful wife and wealth.
So fantastic, so wonderful.
His excitement is contagious.
First one man, then another, in shock and bewilderment, thrusts out his hand.
Each one receives the same sort of prediction from Desnos.
Long life, children, wealth, exciting career, beautiful surroundings, peace, happiness, success, joy, and joy unending.*
*As Desnos reads, palm after palm, the atmosphere of the moment, drop by drop at first, and then, as if in a sudden tidal wave, breaking all at once, completely transforms.
The prisoners are smiling, laughing, clapping one another on the back, their burdens lifted, their reality transformed.
And even more astonishing, the guards are affected.
Like the prisoners, they have been living a dark spell in which marching men to slaughter was a normal and accepted everyday occurrence.
But now, in the middle of this absurd and unprecedented event, the sudden and gratuitous evocation of an alternate reality, the spell is broken.
The guards are disoriented, confused.
The reality they had been living in a moment ago suddenly seems cast into doubt, all but shattered, turned upside down.
They're no longer sure what is real and what is not.
Perhaps their better natures, long suppressed in an effort to conform to Nazi madness that defined the world,*
*long numb to the grief, guilt, and horror, were stirred by Desnos' powerful commitment to the absurd, or perhaps the not absurd, vision.
Who knows?
They are in any case so undone by the jolly scene in front of them that they no longer know what to do.
They can't go through with the executions today.
So they march the prisoners back onto the truck bed and drive them back to the barracks.
Through the spontaneous exercise of imagination, precisely the sort of move that Desnos makes constantly in his poetry, he and his men were saved from execution.
Desnos survived the camps but sadly did not survive the war.
He died of typhus a few days after the liberation.
I heard this story from the poet Alan Bernheimer, a translator of Desnos, and he got it from the writer Susan Griffin.
And she heard it from her friend Odette, herself a writer and a survivor of the Holocaust.*
*When I first heard it, I was tremendously moved.
Then I thought, is this true?
Does this really happen?
It sounds a bit too good to be true, doesn't it?
I don't know Susan Griffin, but I contacted her to ask, and she said she believed it.
Odette, Susan told me, didn't witness the event, but she had heard of it from people who said that they had.
And so for weeks I carried this story in my heart, like a Zen koan, wondering about it, turning it over and over in my mind.
One day I had a realization.
Of course this story is true.
Definitely, absolutely true.
One way or another, it happened.*
*Because the imagination is powerful.
It creates its own self-validating truth, strong enough to affect inner and outer transformation.
When I say I'm absolutely certain this story of Robert Desnos is true, I don't mean I'm certain of it as an objectively verifiable occurrence like history.
I mean that the story as a story is certainly true.
I feel its truth and it changes me, because it expresses something essential about who we are as human beings.*
And he goes on, this is the way he introduces the six paramitas.
They're ultimately imaginative, creative acts.
So I guess that's what we get for having a founding teacher who's also a poet.
And it feels true, doesn't it?
We get in our groove and in our rut and have our way of thinking about things, and we forget that this is an imagined act.
It's possible to evoke imagination and imagine other possibilities.
Like the possibility of awakening, right?
Or like the possibility in the sutra, the service we just did, of transferring the merit to all beings, and receiving merit from the Buddha and Mahaprajapati and all these great ancestors.
Being part of this cosmic darn wheel, right?
It's a vast imaginative act.
That's probably why all cultures have some kind of spirituality, right?
It's a way of evoking imagination and having a bigger-than-self sense of reality.
Like all teenagers, and people at all ages, feel sometime or another that it can't just be this, right?
It can't just be me and these tasks, these responsibilities.
It's got to be more.
So imagination brings us to the more.
Then imagination guided by ethical precepts and an ethical path, right?
The bodhisattva path, this devotion to service, helps us to imagine a better world.
You can imagine all kinds of worlds, right?
So it helps us to imagine a better world.
So I recommend the book.
It'll be fun for everybody to study the six paramitas through July and the rest of our imagined lives.
What came to me when I was thinking about this earlier was the great Tibetan meditation practice of tong len, which is a fabulously and overtly imaginative act.
I'll sketch it out for you in case you haven't done it before.

I learned this from Norman, too, who studied it when he was investigating the mind training slogans of Tibetan Buddhism, which he said he did because he felt Zen does not overtly talk about compassion enough.
So this is a great compassion meditation, tong len.
The word is just a two-word compound in Tibetan.
It means sending and receiving, or receiving and sending.
I always have to look up which is which, tong versus len.
It doesn't matter too much.
In this practice, we imagine suffering, and suffering, as you know, in Buddhism has all these layers.
It's not just terrible, awful pain.
It's down to just subtle feelings of dissatisfaction, basically fine, but, you know, that feeling.
So tong len imagines suffering as stuff, as a substance, a tangible substance, but not too tangible.
Usually it's imagined as thick, dark smoke or mist, often black in color.
I've gotten a little nervous about saying it's black in color because, of course, it was Tibetan, it created a whole other culture in time, but black and white, black is evil.
How was that for our dear African-American brothers and sisters?
But anyway, traditionally it's imagined as black in color.
So it exists and it's in people, it's in the atmosphere, it's in the environment.
And we can help with it by breathing it in.
Humans become these walking transformation factories who can breathe in this tangible suffering, and especially breathe it into our hearts, the area around the heart.
Then in the heart, it's transformed.
It's the [unclear: "biggest dimension of act of all"], you know.
It's transformed, it's healed, it's turned around, it becomes, expresses as light, white light or golden light, or a feeling of healing or a feeling of love.
So that's pretty imaginative.
I always feel with these things, who knows if it really helps the people we're imagining, but it can't hurt.
There is some kind of fringy scientific evidence that maybe it does affect other people, studies of prayer and distance communication and stuff like that, and meditation.
I've been to a few presentations of such papers myself.
The people who present them are very convinced.
But does that matter?
I don't know, because it definitely helps us and definitely heals us.
It definitely changes our perception of reality, to bring suffering more into the fore, that it's a thing and it's in us and it's this black smoke stuff and we can heal it and breathe it out.
So I thought I'd lead you in a take on that meditation, and then we'll have a little chat afterwards and see what you notice.
We've been sitting around for a little while already.
Maybe you want to have a little stretch before we do that.
We're standing up, as is of course allowed.
You can also do the standing if the body's not too tolerant of sitting all this time.
Or lying down, actually.
If there's somewhere comfortable to lie down near where you can hear, why not?
It's probably one to be more on the comfortable end.
This is not a high-concentration practice, it requires concentration, but it's a different thing than staying utterly still and present on your breathing.
It's a more fluid thing, so be comfortable.
So I invite us to close the eyes or lower the gaze.
But this might be one to really close your eyes.
Usually in zazen our eyes are slightly open, but it's probably a good one to close the eyes.
We start by just stabilizing, feeling breath and body.
Let these more complicated cultivation practices really rest on the base that we're always cultivating in zazen: stability and concentration.
Then we'll start with compassion for some of our own suffering.
So in a very open and relaxed way, scanning your own personal experience right now.
This is meditation, so it's about the present.
Just noticing if there is anything, or what are the many things in your present experience that aren't so great.
Feelings or thoughts or sensations in the body that are tense or worried or unhappy in some way or painful.
Landing on some example or a little collection of areas of difficulty in you.
Suffering sounds sort of intense, but it's referred to as suffering.
Can you let whatever that is take shape?
A very solid shape, a fluid shape.
Maybe manifesting as smoke or mist.
Maybe dense and gooey.
Maybe dark in color or gray in color.
Just feel how that changes your experience, to imagine the suffering as a substance like this.
Then with your breathing, first let the breath be pretty full and really be felt in the upper chest.
The quality of breathing into the heart.
Not to make a forced breath, but like inviting a full, heart-centered breath.
It should still be natural and flowing.
Then, probably pretty gently at first, breathing in some, or a little tendril maybe, of the suffering that's in you into your heart center.
So gently and organically breathing it in.
Feeling how it lands in your chest and in your heart.
It would be understandable if that was uncomfortable.
Probably real.
Then powerfully imagining that the heart knows how to transform that, how to turn it around from goopy ickiness to light and warmth and healing and love.
And the exhale sends it back out.
Imagine all of this happening as if the breath were not going through the nose, but coming right into the heart.
Breathing in the suffering into the heart.
Breathing out, healing, release, kindness, whatever form it takes.
You don't even have to name it, just a feeling.
A light, warm, lovely feeling.
So let's just try that for a while with our own suffering.
The suffering in you may move around or shift a little bit.
It may be hard to access this, or easy sometimes.
There may be resistance, as normal.
Really accepting whatever happens.
Breathing in your own suffering.
Transforming it in the heart.
Breathing out, healing.
Gentle, steady effort.
Feeling how it feels all through this cycle.
You can modulate.
You can breathe in more suffering or less.
More energy into the transformation and the exhale.
The creative thing.
We shift our focus a little bit.
Maybe we're still in some way breathing in our own suffering.
It's a kind thing to do for ourselves.
Why don't we invite into our minds someone else we know?
Someone else we know who is suffering in some way.
Could use some compassion or some relief.
Some help with their suffering.
Once you think of somebody, really imagining them.
Inviting that person here into the practice with you.
Tuning in in some way to their suffering, their challenge, their discomfort.
Maybe you know the story of it, but it's not so much about the story.
Just dropping into their experience as best you can.
Imaginative.
And feeling it.
Feeling where their heart is not at rest, or where they're worried or where they're in pain.
Just before imagining the presence of that suffering, some kind of mist or smoke.
Maybe it's got a color to it.
Maybe a density or a stickiness.
Are you willing to breathe some of that into your heart?
And transform it.
Send back healing.
Like a suffering dialysis machine or something.
Really giving yourself over to this creative act and not worrying too much about whether it's practical or makes any sense.
This isn't about that right now.
It's a felt thing.
It's an emotional thing.
Creative thing.
Breathing in the suffering of this other.
Breathing out healing and light.
Just gently maintaining.
When you visualize this stream of the suffering coming from your person into you.
Feeling how it feels to receive the suffering.
And feeling a transformation.
And releasing it back out.
Maybe giving that healing or light or love right back to this person.
It's okay to feel a lot or to not feel much at all.
Lots of layers.
Lots of layers to what's happening.

So many people are suffering, right?
So just deciding what you want to pick off and chew here.
You want to breathe in the suffering of everyone here in our sangha.
At least a little bit of it.

You want to focus on a particular group that you know to be suffering, even if you don't know much about the individuals involved.

So breathing in the suffering of a group of people.
Maybe a few, maybe many.
Let your imagination and instincts guide you.
Maybe everyone in a particular community that you know.
Imagine many little threads flowing, smoke or mist coming from all those people.
Gathering together in your heart.
Transforming.
Radiating out.
Breathing in the suffering of beings.
Transforming it.

Can you bring some energy to this without getting tense?
So there's an organicness to it.
A fluidity.
A naturalness.

I have actually a little bit of formal training in this, but not enough, really.
Probably to do it justice, but maybe enough to introduce us to it.
Anyone want to say a few words about what your experience was like?
